mcqs.question: How does a Kafka topic's append-only log differ from a traditional message queue where messages are removed once consumed?
options: It doesn't differ — both models delete a message after one consumer reads it
Multiple independent consumers can read the same log at their own pace and position, since reading never removes or modifies records
An append-only log can only ever have one consumer at a time
Append-only logs cannot guarantee any ordering at all
mcqs.explanation: Because reading a Kafka log doesn't remove records, many consumers — or consumer groups — can each track their own independent position and read at their own pace, which a delete-on-consume queue doesn't support. Kafka does guarantee order within a partition, and it explicitly supports many concurrent consumers, not just one.

mcqs.question: A pipeline needs every event for a given user processed in the order it was produced. What partitioning key choice achieves that?
options: No key at all, using round-robin partitioning for even load
A random key generated per event
Keying by user_id, so every event for that user always lands on the same partition
Keying by event timestamp
mcqs.explanation: Order is only guaranteed within a partition, and a hash of user_id sends every event for that user to the same partition consistently — that's what preserves per-user order. Round-robin or a random key would spread a single user's events across partitions with no ordering guarantee, and timestamp keying wouldn't group by entity at all.

mcqs.question: Two different consumer groups read the same Kafka topic. What happens to their read positions?
options: They must share the same offset, since only one group can read a topic at a time
The second group can only read data the first group hasn't consumed yet
Reading from two groups causes a rebalance in both groups continuously
Each group tracks its own offsets independently, so one group's progress doesn't affect the other's
mcqs.explanation: Consumer groups are fully independent — each tracks its own offsets, so multiple groups can read the same topic at completely different paces without interfering with each other. Reading doesn't remove data, so there's no 'already consumed' restriction between groups, and simply having two groups doesn't itself trigger rebalances.

mcqs.question: A consumer processes a batch of records, then crashes before committing its offset. What happens on restart, under Kafka's default at-least-once behavior?
options: The consumer reprocesses the same batch again, since the offset was never committed
The consumer resumes after the crashed batch, skipping it entirely
The topic automatically deletes the unprocessed batch
The consumer group is permanently disbanded
mcqs.explanation: Since the offset commit is what marks a batch as done, a crash before committing means the consumer resumes from the last committed offset and reprocesses that batch — safe against loss, but capable of duplicating output. Records aren't skipped or deleted, and a crash doesn't disband the group.

mcqs.question: A producer sets acks=all before writing to a partition. What does that guarantee, and what's the cost?
options: The write is acknowledged only once every in-sync replica has it, which is more durable but slower than acks=1
The write is acknowledged as soon as any single broker receives it, whether leader or follower
acks=all disables replication entirely for that write
acks=all guarantees exactly-once semantics on its own
mcqs.explanation: acks=all waits for every in-sync replica to have the write before acknowledging, so the write survives a leader failure — at the cost of added latency versus acks=1, which only waits on the leader. It doesn't disable replication, and durability settings alone don't provide exactly-once, which requires the separate transactional mechanism.

mcqs.question: A topic has 4 partitions and the team scales its consumer group to 10 instances hoping for more parallelism. What happens?
options: All 10 consumers process every partition simultaneously for extra redundancy
Kafka automatically creates 6 more partitions to accommodate the new consumers
Only 4 consumers get a partition assignment; the other 6 sit idle since partition count caps parallelism within a group
The extra consumers cause the topic's retention policy to reset
mcqs.explanation: Partition count is a hard ceiling on parallelism within one consumer group — with only 4 partitions, at most 4 consumers can have an assignment at once, and the rest remain idle. Kafka doesn't auto-create partitions to match consumer count, and none of this affects retention.
